decks.title: Theory of Consumer Behaviour — Part 1: Utility, Budget Line and Indifference Curves
goals: Compute marginal utility from total utility and state the law of diminishing marginal utility
Find consumer equilibrium for one good and for two goods
Draw the budget line and compute its shifts and rotations
Explain indifference curves, the marginal rate of substitution and equilibrium at the tangency

slides.heading: Utility and the Consumer
slides.body_md: Part 1: how a consumer decides what to buy, by **utility** and by **indifference curves**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: utility, consumer equilibrium, the budget line, indifference curves and the tangency equilibrium
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: A consumer has limited income and many wants. This part shows how she decides what to buy. First we measure satisfaction as utility and find the best choice for one good and for two goods. Then we draw the budget line, introduce indifference curves, and find the equilibrium where the two touch.

slides.heading: Utility, total utility and marginal utility
slides.body_md: **Utility** is the satisfaction a consumer gets from a good. **Total utility (TU)** is the satisfaction from all units consumed; **marginal utility (MU)** is the change in total utility from one more unit: MU = change in TU.

visual.alt: Table of the imagined samosa schedule of Meera: total utility 0, 40, 70, 90, 100, 100, 90 and marginal utility 40, 30, 20, 10, 0, -10 for 0 to 6 samosas
visual.caption: Imagined student Meera. Marginal utility is the change in total utility.

slides.narration: Utility is the satisfaction a consumer gets from a good. Total utility is the satisfaction from all the units she has consumed. Marginal utility is the extra total utility from one more unit. Meera, an imagined student, eats samosas. Her total utility rises from 70 to 90 for the third samosa, so its marginal utility is 20.

slides.heading: The law of diminishing marginal utility
slides.body_md: As more units of a good are consumed, other things unchanged, **MU falls**. When MU reaches zero, TU is at its **maximum** (100 utils); after that MU is **negative** and TU falls.

visual.alt: Two curves drawn from the imagined samosa schedule of Meera: total utility rises to a maximum of 100 utils and then falls, and marginal utility falls from 40 through zero at the fifth samosa to -10
visual.caption: Imagined schedule. TU: 0, 40, 70, 90, 100, 100, 90 utils for 0 to 6 samosas. MU: 40, 30, 20, 10, 0, -10.

slides.narration: The left curve shows total utility rising, reaching its highest point of 100 at the fifth samosa, and then falling. The right curve shows marginal utility falling at every step: 40, 30, 20, 10, then zero. At zero, total utility is at its maximum. After that marginal utility is negative. This is the law of diminishing marginal utility.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: from total to marginal utility
slides.body_md: Find the marginal utility of each of Meera's samosas.
bullets: Step 1: **MU = TU of this unit − TU of the unit before.**
Step 2: The first four give 40, 30, 20, 10 utils: falling.
Step 3: The fifth gives 100 − 100 = **0**; the sixth gives 90 − 100 = **-10**.

visual.alt: Worked table of the marginal utility of each samosa of Meera: 40, 30, 20, 10, 0, -10, falling at every step, zero for the fifth and negative for the sixth
visual.caption: Imagined student Meera.

slides.narration: Subtract the total utility before from the total utility after. The first four samosas give marginal utilities of 40, 30, 20 and 10. The fifth samosa adds nothing, so its marginal utility is zero and total utility is at its peak. The sixth reduces total utility from 100 to 90, so its marginal utility is negative ten.

slides.heading: Quick check: negative marginal utility
slides.body_md: Interpret a fall in total utility.
slides.narration: Look at what happens to total utility when the extra samosa is eaten. If total utility falls, the change attributed to the extra unit is negative. Pick the option that gives the correct sign and the correct meaning.

slides.heading: Consumer equilibrium with one commodity
slides.body_md: A consumer who buys one good is in equilibrium where **MU of the good ÷ its price = MU of a rupee** (MUx ÷ Px). At Rs 4 per samosa and 5 utils per rupee this happens at the **third** samosa.

rows: Buy: worth more than the price
Buy: worth more than the price

visual.alt: Table of the marginal utility per rupee for each of Meera's samosas at Rs 4: 10, 7.5, 5, 2.5, 0, equal to the marginal utility of a rupee (5) at the third samosa
visual.caption: Imagined Meera: one rupee is worth 5 utils.

slides.narration: Meera compares each samosa with the satisfaction of the money she gives up. One rupee is worth 5 utils to her. The price is 4 rupees. For each samosa she divides its marginal utility by the price. The second samosa gives more than 5, so she buys it. The third gives exactly 5, so she stops there. The fourth gives less.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a fall in price
slides.body_md: The price of a samosa falls from Rs 4 to Rs 2.
bullets: Step 1: Required MU = price × MU of a rupee = 4 × 5 = **20** at the old price.
Step 2: At Rs 2 the required MU = 2 × 5 = **10**, which is the fourth samosa.
Step 3: She buys **4** samosas instead of 3.

headers: Required MU = price × MU of a rupee

visual.alt: Table of the equilibrium quantity of samosas of Meera: 3 at Rs 4 and 4 at Rs 2
visual.caption: A lower price means a lower required marginal utility, so more is bought.

slides.narration: At four rupees the required marginal utility is twenty, which belongs to the third samosa. When the price falls to 2 rupees, the required marginal utility falls to 10, which belongs to the fourth samosa. So a lower price makes Meera buy one more samosa, because marginal utility diminishes.

slides.heading: Consumer equilibrium with two commodities
slides.body_md: With two goods the consumer spends her whole income so that **MUx ÷ Px = MUy ÷ Py = MU of a rupee**. This is the law of **equi-marginal utility**: the last rupee yields the same satisfaction on each good.

visual.alt: Table of the marginal utilities and marginal utility per rupee of Meera's samosas (6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1) and juice (5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0)
visual.caption: Imagined Meera: samosa Rs 4, juice Rs 6, income Rs 24.

slides.narration: Meera has 24 rupees for samosas at 4 rupees and juice at 6 rupees. For each unit of each good she works out marginal utility per rupee. The ratios are equal at 4 for the third samosa and the second glass of juice. Buying them costs exactly her whole income, so this is her equilibrium.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: finding the equilibrium bundle
slides.body_md: Compare bundles of samosas and juice for Meera, who has Rs 24.
bullets: Step 1: At (4, 1) the ratios are 3 and 5: unequal, so she should buy more juice.
Step 2: At (1, 3) the ratios are 6 and 3: she should buy more samosas.
Step 3: At (3, 2) both ratios are **4** and the cost is Rs 24: equilibrium, total utility **114**.

rows: Juice gives more per rupee: buy less samosa, more juice
Samosa gives more per rupee: buy more samosa, less juice

visual.alt: Worked comparison of three bundles of Meera: the bundle of 3 samosas and 2 juices has equal ratios 4 and total utility 114; the other two have unequal ratios and lower utility
visual.caption: Total utility 102 at (4, 1) against 114 at the equilibrium bundle.

slides.narration: Test each bundle. With four samosas and one glass of juice, a rupee on juice gives more satisfaction than a rupee on samosas, so she should shift toward juice. With one samosa and three glasses, the reverse holds. With three samosas and two glasses both ratios are 4, and her total utility of 114 is the highest of the three.

slides.heading: Quick check: the equilibrium condition
slides.body_md: State the condition for a single-good consumer.
slides.narration: Recall that a consumer buying one good compares what the last unit is worth with what she pays for it. Marginal utility divided by price is the satisfaction per rupee spent. Choose the option that equates this with the marginal utility of a rupee.

slides.heading: Budget set and budget line
slides.body_md: The **budget line** shows the bundles that cost exactly the income: **P1x1 + P2x2 = M**. Intercepts are **M ÷ P1** and **M ÷ P2**; the slope is **−P1 ÷ P2**. The **budget set** is every affordable bundle, on and below the line.

slides.heading: Shifts and rotations of the budget line
slides.body_md: A change in **income** shifts the line in parallel. A change in **one price** rotates the line about the intercept of the other good.

slides.heading: Preferences and the indifference map
slides.body_md: With **monotonic preferences** the consumer prefers more of at least one good. An **indifference curve** joins bundles of **equal satisfaction**; a set of such curves is an **indifference map**.

visual.alt: An indifference map of an imagined consumer: three convex curves, none crossing another, with the curve farther from the origin showing higher satisfaction
visual.caption: Imagined consumer whose satisfaction is the product of the quantities of good 1 and good 2: curves for 8, 18 and 32.

slides.narration: A consumer with monotonic preferences always prefers a bundle with more of at least one good. An indifference curve joins bundles that give the same satisfaction. Together the curves form an indifference map. The curve that lies farther from the origin holds bundles with more of the goods, so it shows higher satisfaction.

slides.heading: Marginal rate of substitution
slides.body_md: **MRS** is the amount of good 2 a consumer will give up for one more unit of good 1, staying on the same curve. It **diminishes**, so the curve is **convex to the origin**.

visual.caption: Imagined schedule: A (1, 12), B (2, 6), C (3, 4), D (4, 3), E (6, 2). MRS: 6, 2, 1, 0.5.

slides.narration: Meera is equally happy at each of these points. Moving from the first to the second she gives up 6 kilograms of erasers for one more kilogram of pencils. The next steps cost 2, then 1, then 0.5. The rate keeps falling, because the more pencils she has, the less she will give up for another. That makes the curve convex.

slides.heading: Properties of indifference curves
slides.body_md: Indifference curves **slope downward**, a **higher curve** means higher satisfaction, they **never intersect**, and they are **convex** to the origin.

rows: More of one good must be offset by less of the other to keep satisfaction equal
It holds bundles with more of at least one good
A shared bundle would have two satisfaction levels
The marginal rate of substitution diminishes

visual.alt: Table of the four properties of indifference curves and the reason for each
visual.caption: Monotonic preferences: more is preferred to less.

slides.narration: Indifference curves have four properties. They slope downward, because getting more of one good must be offset by less of the other. A higher curve shows higher satisfaction. Two curves never cross, because a common bundle would have two satisfaction levels. And they are convex to the origin, because the marginal rate of substitution diminishes.

slides.heading: Equilibrium at the tangency
slides.body_md: The consumer reaches the **highest indifference curve the budget allows**, where the budget line just touches it. There **MRS = P1 ÷ P2**. For Meera: 3 kg of mangoes and 6 kg of guavas.

visual.alt: Consumer's equilibrium of imagined Meera: the budget line touches the middle indifference curve at point E, 3 kg of mangoes and 6 kg of guavas, where the slope of the curve equals the slope of the budget line; the highest curve cannot be reached
visual.caption: Imagined Meera: income Rs 120, prices Rs 20 and Rs 10. At E the product is 18, MRS 2 equals the price ratio 2.

slides.narration: Meera wants the highest curve she can reach. The curve with the product 32 lies out of reach. The lowest curve is reachable but leaves her worse off than she could be. The middle curve touches the budget line at 3 kilograms of mangoes and 6 of guavas. At that point the slope of the curve equals the slope of the budget line.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: finding the tangency bundle
slides.body_md: Rohan has Rs 200, notebooks cost Rs 25 and pens Rs 10. His satisfaction is the product of the quantities, so MRS = y ÷ x.
bullets: Step 1: Set MRS = price ratio: y ÷ x = 25 ÷ 10, so y = 2.5x.
Step 2: Put this in the budget line: 25x + 10y = 200 gives **x = 4**.

visual.alt: Worked table of the equilibrium of Rohan: 4 notebooks and 10 pens, with satisfaction 40
visual.caption: Imagined Rohan: income Rs 200, notebooks Rs 25, pens Rs 10.

slides.narration: Rohan sets his marginal rate of substitution equal to the price ratio, which is 2.5. That gives pens equal to 2.5 times notebooks. Putting this in the budget line gives 50 times the number of notebooks equal to 200. So he buys 4 notebooks and 10 pens, and spends all of his income.

slides.heading: Quick check: why the curve is convex
slides.body_md: Link the falling MRS to the shape of the curve.
slides.narration: Read the three values of the marginal rate of substitution. They fall as the consumer moves down the curve. Decide what shape of curve has a slope that becomes flatter as you move to the right, and choose the matching option.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Change in total utility from one more unit; it falls, reaches zero at the maximum of total utility
Equilibrium where MU ÷ price equals the marginal utility of a rupee
MUx ÷ Px = MUy ÷ Py = marginal utility of a rupee
P1x1 + P2x2 = M; intercepts M ÷ P1, M ÷ P2; slope P1 ÷ P2
Equal satisfaction; downward, convex, never crossing; higher is better
Tangency of the budget line with the highest curve: MRS = P1 ÷ P2

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: marginal utility, equilibrium with one and two goods, the budget line, indifference curves and the tangency equilibrium

slides.narration: To recap. Marginal utility is the change in total utility and it diminishes. A one-good consumer buys until marginal utility divided by price equals the marginal utility of a rupee. With two goods the ratios are equal. The budget line has intercepts and a slope fixed by income and prices. Indifference curves slope downward, are convex and never cross. Equilibrium is at the tangency, where the marginal rate of substitution equals the price ratio.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Compute **MU = change in TU** and show every step.
For equilibrium, divide MU by price and **compare with the MU of a rupee**.
Write the **budget equation** before the intercepts and slope.
A price change **rotates** the budget line; an income change **shifts** it.
Give **MRS = P1 ÷ P2** as the equilibrium condition and state that the curve is convex.
slides.narration: Some tips. Compute marginal utility by subtracting and show each step. For equilibrium divide marginal utility by price and compare it with the marginal utility of a rupee. Write the budget equation before the intercepts and slope. Remember that a price change rotates the budget line, while an income change shifts it. State that at equilibrium the marginal rate of substitution equals the price ratio.

slides.heading: Demand and Elasticity
slides.body_md: Part 2: **demand** and its determinants, **market demand**, and **price elasticity of demand**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: the demand schedule, determinants of demand, movement and shift, market demand and price elasticity
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: The first part explained how a consumer chooses. This part turns her choices into demand. We define demand, list what determines it, separate a movement along the curve from a shift, add buyers together to get market demand, and measure how strongly buyers respond to a change in price.

slides.heading: Demand and the demand schedule
slides.body_md: **Demand** is the quantity of a good a consumer is **willing and able** to buy at each price over a period. A **demand schedule** lists these quantities.

visual.alt: Table of the imagined demand schedule of Anil for tea: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 cups at prices Rs 10, 8, 6, 4, 2
visual.caption: Imagined tea stall.

slides.narration: Demand is the quantity a consumer is willing and able to buy at each price in a given period. Anil, an imagined regular at a tea stall, buys 2 cups a day when tea costs 10 rupees, and 6 cups when it costs 2. A list of prices and quantities like this is a demand schedule.

slides.heading: The demand curve
slides.body_md: Plotting the schedule gives a **downward-sloping demand curve**: when the price falls, the quantity demanded rises.

slides.heading: The demand function and its determinants
slides.body_md: The quantity demanded depends on the **own price**, the **prices of related goods**, **income**, **tastes and preferences** and **expectations**.

headers: Effect on the demand for tea (imagined stall)
rows: Rise in its price shifts the curve right
Rise in its price shifts the curve left
Normal good: more income shifts right; inferior good: left
Expecting a higher price later shifts demand right now

visual.alt: Table of the determinants of demand for tea and the effect of each on the demand curve
visual.caption: Demand function: the quantity demanded depends on all of these.

slides.narration: Quantity demanded depends on several things at once. The good's own price changes the quantity demanded along the same curve. The price of related goods, the income of buyers, their tastes and their expectations change the demand itself, so the whole curve moves. The table lists each determinant for the tea stall.

slides.heading: The law of demand and its reasons
slides.body_md: **Law of demand:** other things unchanged, a fall in price raises the quantity demanded and a rise lowers it. Reasons: **substitution effect**, **income effect** and **diminishing marginal utility**.

headers: Reason for the law of demand
rows: A fall in its own price makes the good cheaper than substitutes, so buyers switch to it
A lower price raises real income, so more can be bought
More units are bought only at a lower price, as the extra satisfaction falls

visual.alt: Table of the three reasons for the law of demand: substitution effect, income effect and diminishing marginal utility
visual.caption: Law of demand: other things unchanged, price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions.

slides.narration: The law of demand says that, other things unchanged, price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions. There are three reasons. A cheaper good is more attractive than its substitutes. A lower price raises real income, so buyers can afford more. And since marginal utility diminishes, buyers take more units only if the price is lower.

slides.heading: Quick check: what demand means
slides.body_md: Pick the correct meaning of demand.
slides.narration: Think about both parts of demand: the buyer must want the good and be able to pay for it. Demand also refers to a period of time and to several prices. Choose the option that includes all of these ideas.

slides.heading: Normal and inferior goods
slides.body_md: For a **normal good** demand rises with income. For an **inferior good** demand **falls** when income rises, because buyers switch to better goods.

rows: Demand falls (30 kg to 22 kg of millet flour for a household whose income rose)
Coarse millet flour in the imagined village of Sarangpur

visual.alt: Table comparing a normal good, whose demand rises with income, with an inferior good, whose demand falls with income
visual.caption: The effect of income on demand.

slides.narration: Income affects demand in different ways. For a normal good, such as fruit juice, demand rises when income rises. For an inferior good, such as coarse millet flour in an imagined village, demand falls when income rises, because households move to better alternatives. Which kind a good is depends on the buyers.

slides.heading: Substitutes and complements
slides.body_md: **Substitutes** are used in place of each other; a rise in the price of one raises demand for the other. **Complements** are used together; a rise in the price of one **lowers** demand for the other.

headers: Price of the related good rises

visual.alt: Table of the effect on tea demand of a dearer substitute (11 to 14 cups at Rs 6) and of a dearer complement (11 to 8)
visual.caption: Imagined tea stall.

slides.narration: Tea and coffee are substitutes. If coffee becomes dearer, buyers switch to tea, and demand for tea rises at every price. Tea and sugar are complements. If sugar becomes dearer, tea with sugar costs more, and demand for tea falls at every price. At six rupees, tea demand moves from 11 cups to 14 in the first case and 8 in the second.

slides.heading: Movement along and shift of the demand curve
slides.body_md: A change in the **own price** causes a **movement along** the curve. A change in any **other determinant** shifts the **whole curve**.

slides.heading: Price elasticity of demand: the percentage method
slides.body_md: **Price elasticity of demand (ed)** = percentage change in quantity demanded ÷ percentage change in price. The ratio is negative for a normal demand curve; it is quoted **without the sign**.

rows: **Percentage change in quantity ÷ percentage change in price**
Negative for a normal demand curve; quoted without the sign

visual.alt: Table of the percentage method: change in quantity, change in price, their ratio as the elasticity, and the sign convention
visual.caption: Compute both changes from the old values.

slides.narration: Price elasticity of demand measures how strongly buyers respond to a change in price. Divide the percentage change in quantity demanded by the percentage change in price, both measured from the old values. Because price and quantity move in opposite directions, the number is negative, and it is usually quoted without the sign.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: computing elasticity
slides.body_md: Apples and salt at Meera's imagined stall.
bullets: Step 1: Apples: quantity -30 per cent, price 20 per cent: ed = 30 ÷ 20 = **1.5**.
Step 2: Salt: quantity -5 per cent, price 20 per cent: ed = 5 ÷ 20 = **0.25**.
Step 3: Above one: elastic. Below one: inelastic.

visual.alt: Worked table of the elasticity of apples (1.5) and salt (0.25) at Meera's stall by the percentage method
visual.caption: Imagined stall.

slides.narration: For apples the price rises by 20 per cent and the quantity falls by 30 per cent, so elasticity is 1.5, which is greater than one. For salt the price also rises by 20 per cent but quantity falls by only 5 per cent, so elasticity is 0.25, less than one.

slides.heading: The five cases of elasticity
slides.body_md: Demand is **perfectly elastic** (infinite), **greater than one**, **unitary** (one), **less than one** or **perfectly inelastic** (zero).

visual.caption: The five cases of the price elasticity of demand.

slides.narration: There are five cases. For perfectly elastic demand the curve is horizontal and any price rise reduces quantity to zero. If elasticity is greater than one, the curve is flat. If it is one, quantity changes by the same percentage as price. If it is less than one, the curve is steep. If demand is perfectly inelastic, the curve is vertical.

slides.heading: The total expenditure method
slides.body_md: Compare **total expenditure** (price × quantity) before and after a price change. Opposite to price: **above one**. Unchanged: **one**. With price: **below one**.

visual.alt: Table of the total expenditure method: expenditure opposite to price means greater than one, unchanged means one, same direction means less than one
visual.caption: Total expenditure = price × quantity.

slides.narration: The total expenditure method needs only the expenditure before and after a price change. If expenditure moves opposite to price, elasticity is greater than one. If expenditure does not change, elasticity equals one. If expenditure moves in the same direction as price, elasticity is less than one.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: using total expenditure
slides.body_md: Three imagined goods.
bullets: Step 1: Tea: price 10 to 8, expenditure 500 to 560: opposite, so **greater than one**.
Step 2: Fish: price 50 to 40, expenditure 5000 to 4400: together, so **less than one**.
Step 3: Bus pass: price 20 to 25, expenditure stays 2000: **equal to one**.

rows: Price down, expenditure up: **greater than one**

visual.alt: Worked table of the total expenditure method: tea expenditure 500 to 560 (greater than one), fish 5000 to 4400 (less than one) and a bus pass 2000 to 2000 (equal to one)
visual.caption: Imagined goods.

slides.narration: Tea falls in price from 10 to 8 and expenditure rises from 500 to 560. They move in opposite directions, so elasticity exceeds one. For fish, price and expenditure both fall, so elasticity is less than one. For the bus pass, expenditure stays at 2000, so elasticity equals one.

slides.heading: What determines elasticity
slides.body_md: Elasticity is higher for **luxuries**, goods with **many substitutes**, goods that take a **large share of income** and over a **longer period**.

rows: A large share of the budget
A longer period, so buyers can adjust

visual.alt: Table of the four determinants of the price elasticity of demand: nature of the good, availability of substitutes, share of income and time period
visual.caption: Imagined fruit stall.

slides.narration: Four things influence elasticity. Necessities such as salt have inelastic demand, while luxuries are more elastic. The more close substitutes a good has, the more elastic its demand. A good that takes a large share of income is more elastic than one that takes a tiny share. And demand is more elastic over a longer period, when buyers have time to adjust.

slides.heading: Quick check: classify the demand
slides.body_md: Read the elasticity of salt.
slides.narration: Compare the percentage fall in quantity with the percentage rise in price. If quantity changes by a smaller percentage than price, the elasticity is below one and demand is inelastic. Be careful not to choose perfectly inelastic, which means no response at all.

rows: Quantity willing and able to buy at each price in a period
Price and quantity move in opposite directions, other things unchanged

Percentage change in quantity ÷ percentage change in price

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 2: demand, the law of demand, movement and shift, market demand, elasticity and the expenditure method

slides.narration: To recap. Demand is the quantity a consumer is willing and able to buy at each price. By the law of demand, price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions. A change in own price moves us along the curve and a change in any other determinant shifts it. Market demand is the horizontal sum of individual demands. Elasticity is the percentage change in quantity divided by the percentage change in price, and it can also be read from total expenditure.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Define demand with **willing and able**, a **price**, and a **period**.
Say whether a change is a **movement** (own price) or a **shift** (other cause).
For market demand, **add quantities at each price**, never prices.
Compute both **percentage changes from the old values** and quote ed without the sign.
For the expenditure method, compare **price and expenditure directions** and name the case.
For a large price change the two methods can differ slightly at the borderline of one; use the method the question names.

For market demand add quantities at each price. For elasticity compute both percentage changes from the old values. For the expenditure method compare the directions of price and expenditure, and name the case.

sections.heading: 1. Utility and marginal utility
sections.body_md:
**Utility** is the satisfaction a consumer gets from consuming a good or service. **Total utility (TU)** is the satisfaction from all the units consumed; **marginal utility (MU)** is the addition to total utility from one more unit, **MU = change in TU**.

The **law of diminishing marginal utility** says that, other things unchanged, MU falls as more of a good is consumed. When MU is zero, TU is at its maximum; when MU is negative, TU falls. For the imagined student Meera, samosas give TU of 0, 40, 70, 90, 100, 100, 90 utils for 0 to 6 samosas, so MU is 40, 30, 20, 10, 0, -10.

key_terms.definition_md: The satisfaction a consumer derives from consuming a good or service.
The total satisfaction obtained from all the units of a good consumed.
The change in total utility from consuming one more unit of a good.
As a consumer consumes more units of a good, the marginal utility from each additional unit falls, other things unchanged.

sections.heading: 2. Consumer's equilibrium by utility analysis
sections.body_md:
A consumer is in **equilibrium** when she has no reason to change her purchases. With **one good**, she buys until **MUx ÷ Px = MU of a rupee** (the marginal utility of money, taken as constant). At Rs 4 per samosa and 5 utils per rupee, the required MU is 4 × 5 = 20, which is the third samosa; at Rs 2 it is 10, which is the fourth.

With **two goods**, equilibrium needs **MUx ÷ Px = MUy ÷ Py = MU of a rupee** (the **law of equi-marginal utility**) and the whole income spent. Meera, with Rs 24, samosas at Rs 4 and juice at Rs 6, reaches it at 3 samosas and 2 glasses of juice, where both ratios are 4.

key_terms.definition_md: The position in which a consumer, given income and prices, has no tendency to change her purchases because her satisfaction is as high as it can be.
A consumer maximises satisfaction by spending so that the marginal utility per rupee is the same for every good.

sections.heading: 3. Budget set and budget line
sections.body_md:
The **budget set** is all the bundles a consumer can afford; its upper boundary is the **budget line**, **P1x1 + P2x2 = M**. The intercepts are **M ÷ P1** and **M ÷ P2**, and the slope is **−P1 ÷ P2**. For Meera (M = 120, P1 = 20, P2 = 10) the intercepts are 6 and 12 and the slope is −2.

A rise in income shifts the line outward in parallel (intercepts 8 and 16 at income 160); a fall shifts it inward. A rise in P1 rotates the line about the intercept on good 2 (mango intercept 4, slope 3); a rise in P2 rotates it about the intercept on good 1 (guava intercept 6, slope 1).

key_terms.definition_md: The set of all bundles of two goods that the consumer can afford at given prices and income.
The set of bundles that cost exactly the consumer's income: P1x1 + P2x2 = M.

sections.heading: 4. Indifference curves and the marginal rate of substitution
sections.body_md:
With **monotonic preferences** a consumer prefers a bundle that has more of at least one good and no less of the other. An **indifference curve** joins bundles that give equal satisfaction; an **indifference map** is a set of such curves.

The **marginal rate of substitution (MRS)** is the amount of good 2 the consumer will give up for one more unit of good 1, staying on the same curve. It diminishes (6, 2, 1, 0.5 in the imagined schedule), so the curve is **convex to the origin**.

Properties: the curves **slope downward**; a **higher curve** shows higher satisfaction; they **never intersect**; they are **convex**.

A curve joining all bundles of two goods that give the consumer equal satisfaction.
The quantity of good 2 a consumer is willing to give up for one more unit of good 1 while remaining equally satisfied.

sections.heading: 5. Equilibrium with indifference curves
sections.body_md: The consumer reaches the **highest indifference curve the budget line allows**. At that point the budget line **touches** the curve (tangency), so **MRS = P1 ÷ P2**. Meera's best bundle is 3 kg of mangoes and 6 kg of guavas: MRS = 6 ÷ 3 = 2, equal to the price ratio 2. Other affordable bundles, such as (2, 8) and (4, 4), lie on a lower curve, and a higher curve cannot be reached.

sections.heading: 6. Demand, its determinants and market demand
sections.body_md:
**Demand** is the quantity of a good a consumer is willing and able to buy at each price in a given period. The **demand function** relates quantity demanded to the **own price**, **prices of related goods** (substitutes, complements), **income**, **tastes and preferences** and **expectations**.

The **law of demand**: other things unchanged, price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions. Reasons: the **substitution effect**, the **income effect** and **diminishing marginal utility**. For a **normal good** demand rises with income; for an **inferior good** it falls.

A change in the own price causes a **movement along** the demand curve; a change in any other determinant **shifts** it. **Market demand** is the **horizontal sum** of the individual demands: with Anil, Bela and Charu it is 3, 7, 11, 15, 19 cups at prices Rs 10, 8, 6, 4, 2.

key_terms.definition_md: The quantity of a good that a consumer is willing and able to buy at each price during a given period.
Other things unchanged, the quantity demanded of a good rises when its price falls and falls when its price rises.
Goods that can be used in place of each other; a rise in the price of one raises the demand for the other.
Goods that are used together; a rise in the price of one lowers the demand for the other.
The sum of the quantities demanded by all buyers in the market at each price.

sections.heading: 7. Price elasticity of demand
sections.body_md:
By the **percentage method**, **ed = (percentage change in quantity demanded) ÷ (percentage change in price)**, both measured from the old values. The ratio is negative for a normal demand curve; it is quoted without the sign. For imagined apples, quantity falls 30 per cent when price rises 20 per cent: ed = 1.5.

The five cases: **perfectly elastic** (infinity, horizontal curve), **greater than one**, **unitary** (equal to one), **less than one**, **perfectly inelastic** (zero, vertical curve).

By the **total expenditure method**: expenditure moving **opposite** to price means ed is **greater than one**; **unchanged** means **one**; moving **with** price means **less than one**.

Elasticity is higher for luxuries, for goods with many close substitutes, for goods that take a large share of income and over a longer period.

key_terms.definition_md: The responsiveness of the quantity demanded of a good to a change in its own price, measured as the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price.
Price multiplied by the quantity bought.

notes.exam_tips_md:
- Compute **MU = change in TU**; state that MU falls, is zero at maximum TU and negative after.
- Equilibrium: **MUx ÷ Px = MU of a rupee** (one good); **MUx ÷ Px = MUy ÷ Py** (two goods).
- Write the **budget equation**, intercepts **M ÷ P1**, **M ÷ P2** and slope **P1 ÷ P2**.
- Income **shifts** the budget line; a price **rotates** it.
- Equilibrium with curves: **tangency, MRS = P1 ÷ P2**.
- **Movement** (own price) versus **shift** (other determinants); market demand is a **horizontal sum**.
- Elasticity: compute **both percentage changes from the old values**; for the expenditure method compare directions.

cards.back_md: The satisfaction a consumer derives from consuming a good or service.
The total satisfaction from all the units of a good consumed.
The change in total utility from consuming one more unit: MU = change in TU.
As more units of a good are consumed, other things unchanged, the marginal utility of each extra unit falls.
Total utility is at its maximum.
Total utility falls: the extra unit gives dissatisfaction.
MUx ÷ Px = marginal utility of a rupee: the last rupee spent gives the same satisfaction as a rupee kept.
MUx ÷ Px = MUy ÷ Py = marginal utility of a rupee, with the whole income spent.
Spend so that the marginal utility per rupee is equal on every good.
All bundles of two goods the consumer can afford at given prices and income.
The bundles that cost exactly the income: P1x1 + P2x2 = M.

questions.stem_md: When Meera, an imagined student, enjoys a samosa in her college canteen, the satisfaction she gets from it is called

options.text_md: income
utility
demand
opportunity cost

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** utility. Utility is the satisfaction a consumer derives from consuming a good or service. Income is what she earns, demand is the quantity she is willing and able to buy, and opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up.

questions.stem_md: Meera's total utility rises from 70 utils to 90 utils when she eats her third samosa. The 20 utils gained are the

options.text_md: total utility of the third samosa
average utility of three samosas (30 utils)
utility of the first samosa
marginal utility of the third samosa

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** marginal utility of the third samosa. Marginal utility is the change in total utility from one more unit, 90 − 70 = 20 utils. Total utility is the whole 90, and the average over three samosas is 30 utils.

questions.stem_md: At one sitting Meera finds that each further samosa gives her less extra satisfaction than the one before. This tendency is described by the law of

options.text_md: diminishing marginal utility
demand
equi-marginal utility
increasing opportunity cost

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** diminishing marginal utility. The law of diminishing marginal utility says that, other things unchanged, the marginal utility of a good falls as more of it is consumed. The law of demand links price and quantity, the equi-marginal law is about spending across two goods, and increasing opportunity cost belongs to the production possibility frontier.

questions.stem_md: Meera's total utility for 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 samosas her total utility is 0, 40, 70, 90, 100, 100, 90 utils. The marginal utility of her fifth samosa is

options.text_md: 100 utils, the same as total utility
10 utils, as for the fourth samosa
zero, because total utility stops rising at 100 utils
negative, because total utility has fallen

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** zero, because total utility stops rising at 100 utils. MU of the fifth samosa = 100 − 100 = 0. Total utility is at its maximum of 100 utils, so the fifth samosa adds nothing. It becomes negative only for the sixth samosa (90 − 100 = -10).

questions.stem_md: Meera's friends press a sixth samosa on her and her total utility falls from 100 to 90 utils. The marginal utility of the sixth samosa is

options.text_md: positive but smaller than for the fifth
zero, because she has stopped eating
negative (-10 utils): the extra samosa reduces her satisfaction
90 utils, equal to the new total utility

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** negative (-10 utils): the extra samosa reduces her satisfaction. Marginal utility = 90 − 100 = -10 utils. A fall in total utility means that the extra unit gave dissatisfaction, so the marginal utility is negative.

questions.stem_md: Meera buys only samosas, at Rs 4 each, and treats the marginal utility of a rupee as constant. She is in equilibrium when

options.text_md: the marginal utility of the last samosa, divided by its price, equals the marginal utility of a rupee
her total utility is zero
the marginal utility of the samosa is at its highest
the price of a samosa is zero

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the marginal utility of the last samosa, divided by its price, equals the marginal utility of a rupee. A single-good buyer is in equilibrium where MUx/Px equals the marginal utility of money, so that the last rupee spent on the good brings the same satisfaction as a rupee kept. Total utility need not be zero, marginal utility is highest for the first unit, and a zero price would make her buy until marginal utility is zero.

questions.stem_md: Meera has Rs 24 for samosas (Rs 4 each) and juice (Rs 6 a glass). Marginal utilities are 24, 20, 16, 12, 8, 4 utils for the 1st to the 6th samosa, and 30, 24, 18, 12, 6, 0 utils for the 1st to the 6th glass of juice. At 4 samosas and 1 glass of juice she should

options.text_md: buy more samosas and less juice, because MUx/Px is higher
stay where she is, because she has spent most of her money
buy only juice from now on
buy fewer samosas and more juice, because MUy/Py is 5 but MUx/Px is only 3

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** buy fewer samosas and more juice, because MUy/Py is 5 but MUx/Px is only 3. At this bundle MUx/Px = 12 ÷ 4 = 3 and MUy/Py = 30 ÷ 6 = 5. A rupee spent on juice gives more satisfaction than a rupee spent on samosas, so she should shift spending toward juice until the ratios are equal, which happens at 3 samosas and 2 glasses of juice.

questions.stem_md: Meera has Rs 120 for mangoes at Rs 20 a kilogram and guavas at Rs 10 a kilogram. Her budget line shows

options.text_md: all the bundles that give her the same satisfaction
all the bundles of the two fruits that cost exactly Rs 120
only the bundle she likes best
the quantity of each fruit available in the market

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** all the bundles of the two fruits that cost exactly Rs 120. The budget line is made of the bundles that exhaust the whole income at the given prices. Bundles of equal satisfaction lie on an indifference curve, and the favourite bundle is the equilibrium, not the whole line.

questions.stem_md: Meera's budget set, with Rs 120 to spend on mangoes and guavas, consists of

options.text_md: all the bundles on and below the budget line, which she can afford
only the bundles on the budget line
all the bundles above the budget line
the bundles on the highest indifference curve

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** all the bundles on and below the budget line, which she can afford. The budget set is the collection of bundles that cost no more than the income. Bundles above the line cost more than she has, and indifference curves are not part of the budget set.

questions.stem_md: Meera's pocket money rises from Rs 120 to Rs 160 while mangoes stay at Rs 20 and guavas at Rs 10 a kilogram. Her budget line

options.text_md: rotates about the guava intercept
shifts outward, parallel to the old line, with intercepts 8 kg and 16 kg
shifts inward, parallel to the old line
becomes steeper, with slope 3

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** shifts outward, parallel to the old line, with intercepts 8 kg and 16 kg. Intercepts M/P1 and M/P2 both rise, 160/20 = 8 and 160/10 = 16, while the slope P1/P2 = 2 is unchanged, so the line shifts outward and stays parallel. A rotation needs a change in one price.

questions.stem_md: The price of mangoes alone rises from Rs 20 to Rs 30 a kilogram; Meera's income of Rs 120 and the guava price are unchanged. Her budget line

options.text_md: shifts in parallel with both intercepts falling
rotates about the mango intercept
rotates inward about the guava intercept, which stays at 12 kg, while the mango intercept falls to 4 kg
does not change

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** rotates inward about the guava intercept, which stays at 12 kg, while the mango intercept falls to 4 kg. The guava intercept M/P2 = 12 does not depend on the mango price and stays put. The mango intercept falls from 6 to 4, and the slope P1/P2 rises from 2 to 3, so the line is steeper.

questions.stem_md: An indifference curve of Meera, drawn for mangoes and guavas, joins

options.text_md: the bundles that cost the same amount
the bundles she can just afford
the prices at which she buys the two goods
the bundles of the two goods that give her the same satisfaction

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** the bundles of the two goods that give her the same satisfaction. Every bundle on one indifference curve gives the consumer equal satisfaction. Bundles of equal cost lie on a budget line, which is a different curve.

questions.stem_md: Moving along an imagined indifference curve, Meera's marginal rate of substitution of pencils for erasers is 6, 2, 1 at successive steps. Because it keeps falling, the curve is

options.text_md: concave to the origin
a straight line
upward sloping
convex to the origin

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** convex to the origin. Diminishing MRS means that she gives up fewer erasers for each extra pencil as she has more pencils, so the curve flattens as it goes right: it is convex to the origin. A straight line would have a constant MRS (6 throughout), and an indifference curve with monotonic preferences never slopes upward.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is NOT a property of the indifference curves of a consumer with monotonic preferences?

options.text_md: An indifference curve slopes downward
A higher indifference curve shows a higher level of satisfaction
Two indifference curves of the consumer may cut each other
An indifference curve is convex to the origin

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Two indifference curves of the consumer may cut each other. Two curves cannot intersect: the common bundle would give two different satisfaction levels, which contradicts monotonic preferences. The other three statements are standard properties.

questions.stem_md: Meera, with Rs 120 and prices of Rs 20 (mangoes) and Rs 10 (guavas) a kilogram, buys 2 kg of mangoes and 8 kg of guavas. At this bundle her MRS is 4 kg of guavas per kg of mangoes. She should

options.text_md: buy more guavas and fewer mangoes, because the MRS is higher than one
buy more mangoes and fewer guavas, because she would give up 4 kg of guavas for a kilogram of mangoes but the market asks only 2 kg
stay, because the bundle is on her budget line
buy neither, because her MRS is not equal to one

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** buy more mangoes and fewer guavas, because she would give up 4 kg of guavas for a kilogram of mangoes but the market asks only 2 kg. The bundle is on the budget line (20×2 + 10×8 = 120), but MRS = 4 is above the price ratio 2. She values mangoes more than the market requires, so a swap of guavas for mangoes raises satisfaction until MRS = P1/P2 = 2, which happens at 3 kg of mangoes and 6 kg of guavas.

questions.stem_md: The demand of Anil, a regular at an imagined tea stall, for cups of tea means

options.text_md: the quantities he is willing and able to buy at different prices in a given period
the quantity he wishes to buy without the money to pay for it
the quantity the stall owner would like to sell
the quantity of tea left unsold at the end of the day

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the quantities he is willing and able to buy at different prices in a given period. Demand needs both willingness and ability to pay, and it is a schedule of quantities against prices over a period. A wish without purchasing power is not demand, and the seller side and unsold stock concern supply.

questions.stem_md: Anil buys more cups of tea when the price of a cup falls. Which of the following is a reason for this behaviour?

options.text_md: The tea stall finds tea cheaper to make
Tea becomes cheaper relative to substitutes, so he switches toward tea
Anil develops a taste for tea
Anil receives a higher salary

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Tea becomes cheaper relative to substitutes, so he switches toward tea. The substitution effect is one reason for the law of demand: a fall in its own price makes the good relatively cheaper. Cheaper production concerns supply, and a change in taste or income is a change in another determinant, which shifts the curve instead of moving along it.

questions.stem_md: The incomes of the buyers at the imagined tea stall rise. At the unchanged price of Rs 6 a cup, the market now demands 15 cups instead of 11. This is

options.text_md: a movement down along the same demand curve
an extension of demand caused by a price fall
a leftward shift of the demand curve
a rightward shift of the demand curve

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** a rightward shift of the demand curve. The price is unchanged, so the change in quantity (11 to 15) comes from a change in income, another determinant. That moves the whole curve to the right. A movement along the curve needs a change in the good's own price.

questions.stem_md: When the monthly income of a household in the imagined village of Sarangpur rises from Rs 8,000 to Rs 12,000, it buys 22 kg of coarse millet flour a month instead of 30 kg at the same price. Millet flour is for this household

options.text_md: an inferior good
a normal good
a complement of wheat flour
a good whose price has fallen

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** an inferior good. Demand for an inferior good falls as income rises (30 − 22 = 8 kg less here), because buyers switch to better alternatives. For a normal good demand would rise with income, and no price change has been mentioned.

questions.stem_md: Coffee at the imagined tea stall becomes dearer, and the demand for tea at every price rises by 3 cups. Tea and coffee are

options.text_md: complements
both inferior goods
substitutes
unrelated goods

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** substitutes. When the price of one good rises and demand for the other rises, the two goods are substitutes. For complements, such as tea and sugar, the demand for tea would fall (0, 4, 8, 12, 16 cups here instead of 3, 7, 11, 15, 19).

questions.stem_md: At Rs 4 a cup, Anil buys 5, Bela 6 and Charu 4 cups. The market demand at this price is obtained by

options.text_md: adding the three prices
taking the average of the three quantities, 5 cups
adding the three quantities, 5 + 6 + 4 = 15 cups (horizontal summation)
taking the quantity of the largest buyer only

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** adding the three quantities, 5 + 6 + 4 = 15 cups (horizontal summation). Market demand is the horizontal sum of individual demands at each price: 5 + 6 + 4 = 15 cups. Prices are not added, and an average would not describe the whole market.

questions.stem_md: By the percentage method, the price elasticity of demand of the apples at an imagined fruit stall is

options.text_md: percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price
change in price divided by change in quantity demanded
percentage change in income divided by percentage change in price
total expenditure divided by quantity demanded

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price. Elasticity compares the percentage response of quantity demanded to a percentage change in own price. Absolute changes, income changes and expenditure per unit are different measures.

questions.stem_md: The price of notebooks at an imagined shop falls by 10 per cent and the quantity demanded rises by the same 10 per cent. The price elasticity of demand is

options.text_md: greater than one
less than one
zero
unitary, equal to 1

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** unitary, equal to 1. Elasticity = 10 ÷ 10 = 1 when the two percentage changes are equal in size, so demand is unitary elastic.

questions.stem_md: At Kiran's imagined tea stall a fall in the price of tea from Rs 10 to Rs 8 a cup raises total expenditure on tea from Rs 500 to Rs 560. By the total expenditure method, the elasticity of demand is

options.text_md: less than one, because expenditure moves with price
greater than one, because expenditure moves opposite to price
equal to one, because expenditure has changed
zero, because quantity has changed

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** greater than one, because expenditure moves opposite to price. Price fell while expenditure rose from 500 to 560: they moved in opposite directions, which means elasticity is greater than one. Expenditure moving with price would mean less than one, and no change in expenditure would mean one.

questions.stem_md: At an imagined fruit stall, the demand is likely to be LEAST elastic for

options.text_md: common salt packets, a necessity with no close substitute that takes a tiny share of income
imported cherries, a luxury with many substitutes
a particular brand of biscuits when other brands cost the same
a costly fruit basket bought as a gift

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** common salt packets, a necessity with no close substitute that takes a tiny share of income. Demand is less elastic for necessities, goods with few close substitutes and goods that take a small share of income. Luxuries, brands with close rivals and costly items usually have more elastic demand.

questions.stem_md: At the imagined fruit stall the price of salt rises from Rs 20 to Rs 24 a packet and daily sales fall from 200 to 190 packets, an elasticity of 0.25. Demand for salt is

options.text_md: elastic, because quantity falls when price rises
inelastic, because quantity changes by a smaller percentage than price
unitary, because both quantity and price change
perfectly inelastic, because quantity falls only a little

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** inelastic, because quantity changes by a smaller percentage than price. The price rose by 20 per cent and quantity fell by 5 per cent, so elasticity = 5 ÷ 20 = 0.25, below one. Perfectly inelastic means no change at all in quantity, which is not the case here.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Meera is willing to pay less for her fourth samosa of the day than for her first.

**Reason (R):** The marginal utility of a good falls as the consumer has more of it.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true and R explains A. The most she is willing to pay for a unit is measured by its marginal utility, and that falls as she eats more samosas.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Two indifference curves of the same consumer cannot intersect.

**Reason (R):** Indifference curves are convex to the origin.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both statements are true but R does not explain A. Curves cannot cross because a common bundle would carry two different satisfaction levels; convexity comes from a diminishing marginal rate of substitution and says nothing about intersection.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A fall in the price of tea shifts the demand curve for tea to the right.

**Reason (R):** A fall in the price of tea raises the quantity of tea demanded along the same demand curve.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: a change in the good's own price causes a movement along the curve, not a shift. R is true and describes that movement. Shifts come from other determinants such as income, tastes or prices of related goods.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A consumer who buys two goods is in equilibrium when the marginal utility per rupee is the same for both goods.

**Reason (R):** A consumer is in equilibrium only when the whole income is spent on the cheaper good.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: the equi-marginal condition MUx/Px = MUy/Py = marginal utility of money holds at the best bundle. R is false: the equilibrium bundle usually contains both goods, and the cheaper good alone would leave the ratios unequal.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** When the price of tea falls and demand is elastic, the total expenditure of buyers on tea rises.

**Reason (R):** With elastic demand, the percentage rise in quantity demanded is larger than the percentage fall in price.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true and R explains A. Quantity rises proportionately more than price falls, so price times quantity grows. The tea case with price down 20 per cent and quantity up 40 per cent shows expenditure rising from 500 to 560.

questions.stem_md: True or false? When the marginal utility of Meera's samosas is zero, her total utility from samosas is also zero.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** When marginal utility is zero, total utility is at its maximum (100 utils in the imagined schedule), not zero.

questions.stem_md: True or false? For a consumer who prefers more of a good to less, an indifference curve that lies farther from the origin shows a higher level of satisfaction.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** A higher curve contains bundles with more of at least one good, so the consumer prefers them.

questions.stem_md: True or false? If sugar becomes dearer, the demand curve for tea at the imagined stall shifts to the left (0, 4, 8, 12, 16 cups at Rs 10, 8, 6, 4, 2 instead of 3, 7, 11, 15, 19), because tea and sugar are complements.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Complements are used together, so a rise in the price of one lowers the demand for the other at every price.

questions.stem_md: When marginal utility is zero, total utility is at its ___.
questions.solution_md: Total utility stops rising when the extra unit adds nothing, so it is at its maximum.

questions.stem_md: If a rise in the price of a good lowers the total expenditure on it, the price elasticity of demand is ___ than one.
questions.solution_md: Expenditure moving opposite to price means that elasticity is greater than one.

questions.stem_md: Match each case of price elasticity of demand with its description.

options.text_md: Perfectly elastic demand
Perfectly inelastic demand
Unitary elastic demand
Elasticity greater than one

match_right.text_md: A vertical demand curve; quantity does not respond to price
Total expenditure moves opposite to price
A horizontal demand curve; a tiny price rise reduces demand to zero
Quantity changes by the same percentage as price

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Each case is paired with its standard description.

questions.stem_md: Match each imagined event at the tea stall with its effect on the demand for tea.

options.text_md: The price of tea falls
Buyers' incomes rise (tea is a normal good)
Sugar, a complement, becomes dearer
Coffee, a substitute, becomes dearer

match_right.text_md: Demand curve shifts to the right because buyers switch to tea
Movement down along the same demand curve
Demand curve shifts to the left
Demand curve shifts to the right

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(s), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). An own-price change moves along the curve. Changes in income or in the prices of related goods shift it, in the direction that each effect implies.

questions.stem_md: Arrange the steps of finding how many samosas Meera buys when the price and the marginal utility of a rupee are given.

options.text_md: Stop at the unit where the two are equal and read the quantity
Divide each marginal utility by the price of a samosa
Compare each result with the marginal utility of a rupee
List the marginal utility of each successive samosa

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (d) → (b) → (c) → (a). The marginal utility per rupee spent is compared with the marginal utility of money, and equality gives the equilibrium quantity.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: Arrange the steps of finding the price elasticity of demand by the percentage method from an old and a new price and quantity.

options.text_md: Compare the result with one and name the case
Divide the percentage change in quantity by the percentage change in price
Find the change in price and express it as a percentage of the old price
Find the change in quantity and express it as a percentage of the old quantity

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (d) → (c) → (b) → (a). Both percentage changes are computed from the old values, divided, and the size of the result is compared with one.

questions.stem_md: Meera's total utility from samosas for 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 samosas her total utility is 0, 40, 70, 90, 100, 100, 90 utils. Find the marginal utility of the third samosa.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: TU after three samosas is 90 and after two is 70.
Step 2: MU of the third = 90 − 70 = 20 utils.

questions.stem_md: Meera gets 24 utils of marginal utility from her second glass of juice, which costs Rs 6. Find the marginal utility per rupee spent on that glass.
questions.solution_md: MU per rupee = MUy ÷ Py = 24 ÷ 6 = 4 utils per rupee.

questions.stem_md: Meera's marginal utility of the 1st to 6th samosa is 40, 30, 20, 10 and then 0, -10 utils. A samosa costs Rs 4 and a rupee is worth 5 utils to her. How many samosas does she buy in equilibrium?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: In equilibrium MU of the last samosa = price × MU of a rupee = 4 × 5 = 20 utils.
Step 2: The third samosa has MU 20, so she buys 3 samosas. (The second gives 30, worth more than 20, and the fourth gives 10, worth less.)

questions.stem_md: Meera's marginal utilities for the 1st to 6th samosa are 40, 30, 20, 10 and then 0, -10 utils, and a rupee is worth 5 utils to her. The canteen cuts the price of a samosa from Rs 4 to Rs 2. How many samosas does she now buy in equilibrium?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Required MU = 2 × 5 = 10 utils.
Step 2: The fourth samosa has MU 10, so she buys 4 samosas, one more than the 3 bought at Rs 4.

questions.stem_md: Neha has Rs 180 to spend on notebooks at Rs 15 each and pens at Rs 12 each. What is the horizontal intercept of her budget line, with notebooks on the horizontal axis?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Horizontal intercept = M ÷ P1.
Step 2: 180 ÷ 15 = 12 notebooks (the vertical intercept is 180 ÷ 12 = 15 pens).

questions.stem_md: Rohan has Rs 200, notebooks cost Rs 25 each and pens Rs 10 each. Find the magnitude of the slope of his budget line, with notebooks on the horizontal axis.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Slope = P1 ÷ P2 in magnitude.
Step 2: 25 ÷ 10 = 2.5 pens per notebook (intercepts: 8 notebooks and 20 pens).

questions.stem_md: Meera is equally satisfied by A: 1 kg of pencils and 12 kg of erasers; B: 2 kg of pencils and 6 kg of erasers; C: 3 kg of pencils and 4 kg of erasers; D: 4 kg of pencils and 3 kg of erasers; E: 6 kg of pencils and 2 kg of erasers. Find her marginal rate of substitution when she moves from B to D.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Erasers given up = 6 − 3 = 3 kg.
Step 2: Extra pencils = 4 − 2 = 2 kg.
Step 3: MRS = 3 ÷ 2 = 1.5.

answer.unit: kg of erasers per kg of pencils

marking_scheme.step: Correct answer: 1.5 kg of erasers per kg of pencils

questions.stem_md: Rohan has Rs 200 and buys notebooks at Rs 25 each and pens at Rs 10 each. His satisfaction is the product of the two quantities, for which MRS = y ÷ x (pens per notebook). How many notebooks does he buy in equilibrium?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: In equilibrium MRS = P1 ÷ P2 = 25 ÷ 10 = 2.5, so y = 2.5x.
Step 2: The budget line gives 25x + 10y = 200, so 25x + 10×2.5x = 50x = 200.
Step 3: x = 4 notebooks (and y = 10 pens).

questions.stem_md: At the imagined tea stall, Anil 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, Bela 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 and Charu 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 cups at the prices of Rs 10, 8, 6, 4, 2 per cup. How many cups does the market demand per day at Rs 4? The quantities listed are in the order of the prices 10, 8, 6, 4, 2.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: At Rs 4 Anil buys 5, Bela 6 and Charu 4.
Step 2: Market demand = 5 + 6 + 4 = 15 cups.

questions.stem_md: At Rs 6 a cup the three buyers of the imagined tea stall take 4, 4 and 3 cups. After a rise in their incomes, Anil buys 1 more cup, Bela 2 more and Charu 1 more at every price. What is the market demand at Rs 6 now?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Before the rise, market demand = 4 + 4 + 3 = 11 cups.
Step 2: The shift adds 1 + 2 + 1 = 4 cups at every price.
Step 3: New demand = 11 + 4 = 15 cups.

questions.stem_md: Meera's imagined fruit stall raises the price of apples from Rs 50 to Rs 60 a kilogram, and daily sales fall from 100 kg to 70 kg. Find the price elasticity of demand by the percentage method, ignoring the minus sign.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Change in quantity = (70 − 100) ÷ 100 × 100 = -30 per cent.
Step 2: Change in price = (60 − 50) ÷ 50 × 100 = 20 per cent.
Step 3: Elasticity = 30 ÷ 20 = 1.5.

questions.stem_md: At the imagined fruit stall the price of a packet of salt rises from Rs 20 to Rs 24 and daily sales fall from 200 to 190 packets. Find the price elasticity of demand by the percentage method, ignoring the sign.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Change in quantity = (190 − 200) ÷ 200 × 100 = -5 per cent.
Step 2: Change in price = (24 − 20) ÷ 20 × 100 = 20 per cent.
Step 3: Elasticity = 5 ÷ 20 = 0.25.

questions.stem_md: A stall sells 400 kg of mangoes a day. The price elasticity of demand for mangoes is 2. If the price falls by 5 per cent, how many kilograms will be sold a day afterwards?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Percentage change in quantity = elasticity × percentage change in price = 2 × 5 = 10 per cent rise.
Step 2: Rise = 400 × 10 ÷ 100 = 40 kg.
Step 3: New quantity = 400 + 40 = 440.00000000000006 kg.

questions.stem_md: Explain total utility and marginal utility, using Meera and her samosas as the example, and state how the two are related.
questions.solution_md: TU: whole satisfaction; MU: change in TU per extra unit.

answer.model_answer_md: Total utility is the whole satisfaction Meera gets from all the samosas she eats; marginal utility is the extra satisfaction from one more samosa. Marginal utility is the change in total utility, so MU of the third samosa is 90 − 70 = 20 utils.

marking_scheme.step: Total utility and marginal utility defined
Relation MU = change in TU, with the figure

questions.stem_md: State the law of diminishing marginal utility. Using Meera's marginal utilities of 40, 30, 20, 10 utils for her first four samosas, show how the law operates.
questions.solution_md: Statement and illustration.

answer.model_answer_md: The law says that as a consumer takes more units of a good, the marginal utility from each additional unit falls, other things unchanged. For Meera it falls 40, 30, 20, 10: every extra samosa adds less than the one before, until it reaches 0.

questions.stem_md: Define a budget line. For income Rs 120 and prices Rs 20 and Rs 10 for goods 1 and 2, state its intercepts and slope.
questions.solution_md: Definition, intercepts, slope.

answer.model_answer_md: A budget line shows all the bundles of two goods that the consumer can buy by spending the whole income at the given prices: P1x1 + P2x2 = M. Here the intercepts are 120/20 = 6 units of good 1 and 120/10 = 12 of good 2, and the slope is −20/10 = −2.

marking_scheme.step: Budget line defined with the equation

questions.stem_md: Define the marginal rate of substitution and state what happens to it as a consumer moves down an indifference curve.
questions.solution_md: MRS defined; diminishing.

answer.model_answer_md: The marginal rate of substitution is the amount of good 2 a consumer will give up for one more unit of good 1 while staying on the same indifference curve. It diminishes down the curve: the more of good 1 she has, the less of good 2 she gives up for it.

questions.stem_md: State any two properties of indifference curves of Meera, who prefers more of a good to less, and give the reason for one of them.
questions.solution_md: Any two properties with a reason.

answer.model_answer_md: Her indifference curves slope downward, because taking more of one good must be matched by giving up some of the other to stay equally satisfied. A higher curve shows higher satisfaction, since it contains bundles with more of at least one good. They are also convex and never cut one another.

questions.stem_md: List the main determinants of the demand for tea at an imagined tea stall, and say which of them lies behind a movement along the demand curve.
questions.solution_md: Own price, related goods, income, tastes, expectations; own price moves along.

answer.model_answer_md: Demand depends on the price of tea itself, the prices of related goods (substitutes such as coffee and complements such as sugar), buyers' income, their tastes and preferences, and their expectations. The own price alone causes a movement along the curve; the others shift it.

marking_scheme.step: Own price identified as the cause of movement

questions.stem_md: At the imagined tea stall the market demand at Rs 8 is 7 cups and at Rs 6 is 11 cups. Is this a movement along the curve or a shift? Explain.
questions.solution_md: Own price changed: movement.

answer.model_answer_md: It is a movement along the demand curve. The price of tea itself changed from Rs 8 to Rs 6, and the quantity demanded rose from 7 to 11 cups. A shift would show a different quantity at the same price because another determinant has changed.

marking_scheme.step: Reason: own price changed, not another determinant

questions.stem_md: Define the price elasticity of demand and state its sign convention, using the demand for apples at Meera's imagined stall.
questions.solution_md: Definition and sign.

answer.model_answer_md: Price elasticity of demand measures how responsive the quantity demanded of apples is to a change in their price: the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price. Because the two changes have opposite signs, the number is negative; it is usually quoted without the sign.

questions.stem_md: State any two determinants of the price elasticity of demand and explain how each affects it, with an imagined example from a fruit stall.
questions.solution_md: Any two determinants with effects.

answer.model_answer_md: Availability of substitutes: demand for a particular brand of juice is elastic because other brands can replace it. Nature of the good: salt, a necessity with a tiny share of the budget, has inelastic demand. Time period and share of income also matter.

questions.stem_md: Meera buys samosas at Rs 4 and a rupee is worth 5 utils to her. Using the marginal utilities 40, 30, 20, 10 for the first four samosas, show why she buys 3 samosas and not 4.
questions.solution_md: Equilibrium at the third samosa.

answer.model_answer_md: She buys until MU of the last unit divided by the price equals the marginal utility of money, so MU must be 4 × 5 = 20 utils. The third samosa gives 20, so MU/P = 5 = 5. The fourth gives only 10, so MU/P = 2.5 is below 5: a rupee spent on it brings less than a rupee kept.

marking_scheme.step: Third samosa satisfies it with figures

questions.stem_md: Meera has Rs 24. Samosas cost Rs 4 and juice Rs 6; marginal utilities are 24, 20, 16, 12, 8, 4 utils for the 1st to the 6th samosa, and 30, 24, 18, 12, 6, 0 utils for the 1st to the 6th glass of juice. Show that 4 samosas and 1 glass of juice is not an equilibrium and say what she should do.
questions.solution_md: Unequal ratios; shift to juice.

answer.model_answer_md: At 4 samosas and 1 glass of juice she spends 4×4 + 6×1 = 22 rupees. MUx/Px = 12/4 = 3 but MUy/Py = 30/6 = 5. Since juice gives more satisfaction per rupee, she should buy less of samosas and more juice, moving toward 3 samosas and 2 glasses of juice where both ratios are 4.

marking_scheme.step: Direction of change and equilibrium bundle

questions.stem_md: Meera's budget line has income Rs 120, mango price Rs 20 and guava price Rs 10. Find the intercepts after (i) her income rises to Rs 160, and (ii) the guava price rises to Rs 20, and describe each change.
questions.solution_md: Parallel shift; rotation.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) Both intercepts rise to 160/20 = 8 kg and 160/10 = 16 kg; the line shifts outward in parallel, with slope 2 unchanged. (ii) The mango intercept stays 6 kg while the guava intercept falls to 120/20 = 6 kg; the line rotates inward about the mango intercept and its slope falls to 1.

questions.stem_md: State the law of demand and explain any two reasons for it, with an imagined case of Anil buying tea.
questions.solution_md: Law and two reasons.

answer.model_answer_md: Other things unchanged, a fall in the price of a good raises the quantity demanded, and a rise lowers it. Substitution effect: cheaper tea tempts Anil away from coffee. Income effect: a lower price raises his real income, so he can buy more tea. Diminishing marginal utility also makes him willing to buy more only at a lower price.

marking_scheme.step: Law stated with other things unchanged
Income effect or diminishing marginal utility

questions.stem_md: At Rs 8 a cup Anil, Bela and Charu buy 3, 2 and 2 cups, and at Rs 4 they buy 5, 6 and 4 cups. Find the market demand at each price and say how the market demand curve is obtained.
questions.solution_md: 7 and 15 cups; horizontal summation.

answer.model_answer_md: At Rs 8: 3 + 2 + 2 = 7 cups. At Rs 4: 5 + 6 + 4 = 15 cups. The market demand curve is the horizontal sum of the individual demand curves: at every price the quantities of all buyers are added.

marking_scheme.step: Market demand at the first price
Market demand at the second price

questions.stem_md: At an imagined shop, the price of a bus pass rises from Rs 20 to Rs 25 and sales fall from 100 to 80 passes. Use the total expenditure method to state the elasticity, and give the rule for the other two cases.
questions.solution_md: Expenditure unchanged: unitary.

answer.model_answer_md: Expenditure before = 20 × 100 = Rs 2000; after = 25 × 80 = Rs 2000. It is unchanged, so elasticity is equal to one. If expenditure moves opposite to price, elasticity is greater than one; if it moves in the same direction as price, elasticity is less than one.

marking_scheme.step: Rule for the other two cases

questions.stem_md: Meera's marginal utility of samosas is 40, 30, 20, 10 utils for the first four, then 0, -10. State the law of diminishing marginal utility, show it from these figures, and explain how she decides how many samosas to buy at Rs 4 when a rupee is worth 5 utils.
questions.solution_md: Law, figures, equilibrium at three samosas.

answer.model_answer_md: The law states that, other things unchanged, marginal utility falls as more of a good is consumed. Meera's figures fall from 40 to 10, then 0 and -10, when total utility is at its maximum and then declines. She compares each unit's MU divided by the price with the marginal utility of money: 7.5 exceeds 5 for the second samosa, it equals 5 for the third, and it falls to 2.5 for the fourth. So she stops at 3 samosas, where MUx/Px = 5.

marking_scheme.step: Condition MU/P equals MU of money
Ratios for second to fourth samosa

questions.stem_md: Meera has Rs 24 for samosas at Rs 4 and juice at Rs 6 a glass. The marginal utilities are 24, 20, 16, 12, 8, 4 utils for the 1st to the 6th samosa, and 30, 24, 18, 12, 6, 0 utils for the 1st to the 6th glass of juice. Find her equilibrium bundle using the law of equi-marginal utility and verify that it exhausts her income.
questions.solution_md: Equilibrium bundle (3, 2).

answer.model_answer_md: MU per rupee for samosas is 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 and for juice 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0. The ratios are equal at 4 for the third samosa and the second glass: MUx/Px = MUy/Py = 4. The cost is 4×3 + 6×2 = 24, the whole income. Her equilibrium is 3 samosas and 2 glasses of juice, with a total utility of 114 utils. Any other affordable bundle gives less.

questions.stem_md: Meera has Rs 120 for mangoes at Rs 20 and guavas at Rs 10 a kilogram, and her satisfaction is the product of the two quantities. Explain, with the equilibrium condition, why her best bundle is 3 kg of mangoes and 6 kg of guavas.
questions.solution_md: Tangency, MRS = price ratio.

answer.model_answer_md: The best bundle lies on the budget line and on the highest indifference curve she can reach, where the budget line touches a curve: MRS = P1/P2 = 2. At (3, 6) the product is 18 and the MRS 6/3 = 2. The bundle (2, 8) is also affordable but gives only 16, and any curve above 18, such as 32, cannot be reached. So her equilibrium is at the tangency.

marking_scheme.step: Highest attainable curve touches the budget line

questions.stem_md: Meera has Rs 120 for mangoes (Rs 20 a kg) and guavas (Rs 10 a kg). Write the equation of her budget line, find its intercepts and slope, and show the effect on the line of a rise in her income to Rs 160 and of a rise in the mango price to Rs 30.
questions.solution_md: Equation, intercepts, slope, shift, rotation.

answer.model_answer_md: The budget line is 20x1 + 10x2 = 120, with intercepts 6 kg of mangoes and 12 kg of guavas and slope −2. A rise in income to Rs 160 shifts it out in parallel: intercepts 8 and 16, slope unchanged. A rise in the mango price rotates it inward about the guava intercept 12: the mango intercept falls to 4 and the slope becomes −3.

marking_scheme.step: Income rise: parallel shift with figures
Mango price rise: rotation with figures

questions.stem_md: The imagined tea stall's market demand is 3, 7, 11, 15, 19 cups at prices of Rs 10, 8, 6, 4, 2. Explain the difference between a movement along the demand curve and a shift of the curve, using (i) a fall in price from Rs 8 to Rs 6 and (ii) a rise in buyers' incomes that adds 4 cups at every price.
questions.solution_md: Movement versus shift with figures.

answer.model_answer_md: A movement along the curve is caused only by a change in the good's own price: when the price falls from Rs 8 to Rs 6, quantity rises from 7 to 11 cups on the same curve. A shift is caused by another determinant, such as income. A rise in incomes adds 4 cups at every price, so at Rs 6 demand becomes 15 cups and the whole curve moves right, from 3, 7, 11, 15, 19 to 7, 11, 15, 19, 23.

questions.stem_md: Meera's imagined stall sells apples (price Rs 50 to Rs 60, quantity 100 kg to 70 kg) and fish (price Rs 50 to Rs 40, quantity 100 kg to 110 kg). Find the elasticity of each by the percentage method and confirm each result by the total expenditure method.
questions.solution_md: Apples 1.5; fish 0.5.

answer.model_answer_md: Elasticity by the percentage method is the percentage change in quantity divided by the percentage change in price, taken without the sign. Apples: quantity falls 30 per cent while price rises 20 per cent, so elasticity = 30 ÷ 20 = 1.5, above one. Expenditure falls from 5000 to 4200 as price rises, which confirms it. Fish: quantity rises 10 per cent while price falls 20 per cent, so elasticity = 10 ÷ 20 = 0.5, below one. Expenditure falls from 5000 to 4400 together with price, which confirms it.
